titleEn: I love You, LORD, my strength
progression: | Dm Dm | Bb C | Dm Gm | A A |
intro: Fifty-one verses, the longest psalm in the first book of the Psalter, and a royal thanksgiving built like a report: I was drowning, God came down in a storm, God pulled me out, and here is what I did afterwards. A second copy of this poem stands in the Bible as 2 Samuel 22, and the two versions differ from each other in wording and spelling throughout. For a learner it is the best single training ground for the object suffix on a verb: the -ni ending, me, lands on more than twenty verbs here, and once you hear it you can read half the Psalter. The middle section, verses 8 to 16, is a storm theophany, so the vocabulary is weather and geology rather than prayer.

stichs.en: For the choirmaster. Of the servant of the LORD, of David,
who spoke to the LORD the words of this song
on the day the LORD rescued him from the grip of all his enemies, and from the hand of Saul.

verses.summary: The heading dates the poem to a single day, after every enemy and Saul in particular. It also calls David a servant before it calls him a king, which is the psalm's own ranking.

stichs.en: And he said:
I love You, LORD, my strength.

verses.summary: The opening is a declaration rather than a request, and the verb chosen for it is not the ordinary verb for love. Everything after this is the reason.

stichs.en: The LORD is my crag, my stronghold and my deliverer,
my God, my rock in whom I take refuge,
my shield, the horn of my salvation, my high tower.

verses.summary: Eight titles in one verse, and seven of them carry the same possessive ending, -i, my. The images are all defensive terrain: rock, fort, tower, the places a hunted man goes.

stichs.en: I call on the LORD, who is praised,
and from my enemies I am saved.

verses.summary: The line compresses the whole psalm into six words: calling and being saved, with praise standing before both. The final verb is passive, which matters given what the speaker claims later.

stichs.en: The cords of death encircled me,
and torrents of destruction terrified me.

verses.summary: The danger arrives as water and rope, not as an army. Both verbs end in -ni, me, and that suffix will now repeat for the next fifteen verses.

stichs.en: The cords of Sheol surrounded me,
the snares of death confronted me.

verses.summary: The same picture again with the words crossed over, so that death opens one line and closes the other. The trap closes; there is no exit left in the grammar.

stichs.en: In my distress I call on the LORD,
and to my God I cry out.
From His palace He hears my voice,
and my cry before Him comes into His ears.

verses.summary: The hinge of the first half. Two verbs of shouting from below are answered by two organs of hearing above, and nothing else happens in the verse.

stichs.en: Then the earth heaved and quaked,
the foundations of the mountains shuddered and were shaken,
because He was burning with anger.

verses.summary: The answer to the cry is not a word but an earthquake. Note that the cause is given last, so the reader feels the shaking before learning why.

stichs.en: Smoke went up from His nostrils,
and fire from His mouth devoured,
coals blazed out from Him.

verses.summary: Anger is described physically because the Hebrew idiom for anger is a burning nose. The verse simply takes the idiom literally and lets smoke come out.

stichs.en: He bent the heavens and came down,
and thick darkness was under His feet.

verses.summary: The sky is treated as a fabric that can be pushed down. The descent is the first movement toward the speaker, and it is made in the dark.

stichs.en: He rode on a cherub and flew,
He swooped on the wings of the wind.

verses.summary: The cherub is a mount here, not a decoration on the ark. The second line repeats the first with wind in place of the creature, which is how biblical poetry gives a thing two names.

stichs.en: He makes darkness His hiding place,
around Him His shelter,
darkness of waters, thick clouds of the skies.

verses.summary: The rescuer arrives concealed. Darkness is not an obstacle to Him but a tent He puts up, which is the opposite of how darkness works for the speaker.

stichs.en: From the brightness before Him His clouds passed through,
hail and coals of fire.

verses.summary: Light breaks the cloud cover from inside. Hail and fire arrive together, which is the standard biblical pairing for weather used as a weapon.

stichs.en: The LORD thundered in the heavens,
and the Most High gave forth His voice,
hail and coals of fire.

verses.summary: Thunder is named as a voice, which answers verse 7: the speaker's voice went up and this comes back down. The last three words repeat verse 13 exactly.

stichs.en: He sent out His arrows and scattered them,
lightnings in abundance, and He routed them.

verses.summary: The storm becomes artillery, and for the first time the enemies reappear as a plural object, them. They are never described, only dispersed.

stichs.en: Then the channels of waters were seen,
and the foundations of the world were laid bare,
at Your rebuke, LORD,
at the blast of the breath of Your nostrils.

verses.summary: The sea bed is exposed, which in biblical language means the world has been taken apart to its floor. This is also the verse where the psalm switches to addressing God as You.

stichs.en: He reached from on high and took me,
He drew me out of many waters.

verses.summary: After nine verses of cosmic machinery, the whole apparatus reduces to one hand and one person. The waters of verse 5 are still there; only the speaker has moved.

stichs.en: He rescues me from my strong enemy, and from those who hate me,
for they were stronger than me.

glosses: and from those who hate me
verses.summary: The admission is the point: the enemy really was the stronger party. The psalm does not claim the fight was fair, only that it was won.

stichs.en: They confronted me on the day of my disaster,
but the LORD was a support for me.

verses.summary: The verb that death used in verse 6 comes back with human enemies as its subject. The day of disaster is answered by the day of rescue named in the heading.

stichs.en: He brought me out into the open, He set me free,
because He delighted in me.

verses.summary: Rescue is described as space. The word for the open place is built on the root for wide, the exact opposite of the distress in verse 7, which is built on the root for narrow.

stichs.en: The LORD repaid me according to my righteousness,
according to the cleanness of my hands He returned to me.

verses.summary: A second explanation begins, and it sits awkwardly next to the first. Verse 20 said He delighted in me; this says I had earned it.

stichs.en: For I have kept the ways of the LORD,
and have not turned away wickedly from my God.

verses.summary: The claim is stated positively then negatively, which is how biblical Hebrew makes a legal defence. The speaker is arguing a case, not confessing.

stichs.en: For all His judgments were before me,
and His statutes I did not put away from me.

verses.summary: Two legal words, judgments and statutes, enter a poem that so far has used only weather and terrain. The register changes with the argument.

stichs.en: I was blameless with Him,
and I kept myself from my guilt.

verses.summary: Blameless here means whole or undivided rather than sinless, and the second verb is reflexive: the guarding was work the speaker did on himself.

stichs.en: So the LORD returned to me according to my righteousness,
according to the cleanness of my hands in His eyes.

verses.summary: Verse 21 comes back almost word for word, closing the argument as a frame. The only addition is in His eyes, which quietly moves the verdict off the speaker.

stichs.en: With the faithful You show Yourself faithful,
with a blameless man You show Yourself blameless.

verses.summary: The grammar carries the theology: each verb is built from the adjective standing next to it, in the stem that means acting a quality out. God is described as reflecting the person.

stichs.en: With the pure You show Yourself pure,
and with the crooked You show Yourself twisted.

verses.summary: The pattern is pushed to its uncomfortable end. The last pair is deliberately harsh, and translators have argued about it for centuries because it makes God take the shape of a crooked man.

stichs.en: For You save an afflicted people,
but haughty eyes You bring low.

verses.summary: The mirror principle is applied to social position rather than character. Height is the thing being measured, and the psalm will spend its second half raising the speaker.

stichs.en: For You light my lamp,
the LORD my God makes my darkness bright.

verses.summary: The darkness that was God's shelter in verse 12 is now the speaker's, and it gets lit. This is the last quiet verse before the psalm turns military.

stichs.en: For by You I charge a raiding band,
and by my God I leap a wall.

verses.summary: The verbs turn active for the first time since verse 7. Both are physical and specific, one for open field and one for a siege, and both are prefixed with by You.

stichs.en: As for God, His way is blameless,
the word of the LORD is refined,
He is a shield to all who take refuge in Him.

verses.summary: The word for refined is a metalworker's term, used of silver purified in a crucible. The verse turns from David's own case to a general rule, and widens the audience to anyone.

stichs.en: For who is a god apart from the LORD?
And who is a rock besides our God?

verses.summary: Two rhetorical questions, and the pronoun goes plural: our God. The rock of verse 3 comes back, now as the thing nobody else can be.

stichs.en: The God who girds me with strength,
and made my way blameless.

verses.summary: Girding is what you do with a belt before work or battle. The word blameless has now been said of the speaker, of God's way, and of the speaker's way, in that order.

stichs.en: Making my feet like the deer's,
and standing me on my heights.

verses.summary: The image is a hind on rock, sure footed where a man would slip. Height returns from verse 28, but here it is granted rather than punished.

stichs.en: Training my hands for battle,
so my arms bend a bow of bronze.

verses.summary: The hands that were clean in verse 21 are being taught to fight. A bronze bow is beyond ordinary strength, which is the whole claim of the line.

stichs.en: You gave me the shield of Your salvation,
and Your right hand supports me,
and Your gentleness makes me great.

verses.summary: Three gifts, ending on the strangest word in the psalm. Greatness is credited not to the shield or the hand but to God stooping, which reverses everything the war language implies.

stichs.en: You widen my stride beneath me,
and my ankles have not slipped.

verses.summary: The open space of verse 20 becomes room to walk in. Ankles are an oddly precise body part, and that precision is what makes the boast sound like a soldier talking.

stichs.en: I pursue my enemies and overtake them,
and I do not turn back until they are finished.

verses.summary: The reversal is complete: the man who was surrounded in verse 6 is now the one chasing. The verb for pursue is the same one used of hunted prey earlier in the book.

stichs.en: I crush them so they cannot rise,
they fall under my feet.

verses.summary: Under my feet answers under His feet in verse 10, and the parallel is not accidental. This is the most violent verse in the psalm and it is stated flatly.

stichs.en: You girded me with strength for the battle,
You made those who rose against me kneel beneath me.

verses.summary: The credit is handed back mid boast. Every active verb of the last three verses is now retold with You as the subject.

stichs.en: You gave me my enemies' backs,
and those who hate me, I silenced them.

verses.summary: Giving someone the neck is the Hebrew way of saying they turned and ran. The idiom is physical and the translation loses it if you write retreat.

stichs.en: They cry out, and there is no saviour,
to the LORD, but He did not answer them.

verses.summary: The enemies use the same verb the speaker used in verse 7, and get silence. The psalm shows its symmetry at its harshest here, and does not soften it.

stichs.en: I grind them like dust on the face of the wind,
like the mud of the streets I pour them out.

verses.summary: Two images of something reduced until it can no longer be gathered. The wind that carried God in verse 11 now carries the enemy away as powder.

stichs.en: You deliver me from the strife of a people,
You set me as head of nations;
a people I have not known serve me.

verses.summary: The subject widens from one man's enemies to foreign nations, which is where a royal psalm has to end up. Delivered from his own people first, then given others.

stichs.en: At the hearing of an ear they obey me,
foreigners cringe before me.

verses.summary: Obedience arrives by rumour, before any army does. The Hebrew for obey is literally they hear to me, the same verb as God hearing in verse 7.

stichs.en: Foreigners wither,
and come trembling out of their strongholds.

verses.summary: The verb for wither is used of leaves and of clothes wearing out. Their strongholds are the same kind of place the LORD was for the speaker in verse 3, which is the point of the contrast.

stichs.en: The LORD lives!
And blessed is my rock,
and exalted be the God of my salvation,

verses.summary: The closing doxology opens with a two word shout. Rock and salvation both come back from verse 3, so the psalm is deliberately returning to its own beginning.

stichs.en: The God who gives me vengeance,
and subdues peoples beneath me,

verses.summary: Vengeance is given rather than taken, which is the psalm's consistent grammar for anything the speaker does. Beneath me repeats for the third time.

stichs.en: my deliverer from my enemies;
indeed You lift me above those who rise against me,
You rescue me from the man of violence.

verses.summary: The last enemy is a single man of violence, not an army, which brings the psalm back down to the scale of verse 18. The title deliverer repeats from verse 3.

stichs.en: Therefore I thank You among the nations, LORD,
and to Your name I will sing.

verses.summary: The thanks are given in public and abroad, in front of the nations just subdued. Praise is treated as the last act of the campaign, not as a private matter.

stichs.en: He magnifies the victories of His king,
and does kindness to His anointed,
to David and to his seed forever.

verses.summary: The last verse leaves the first person entirely and speaks of David in the third, extending the promise past his lifetime. This line is said daily in the Grace after Meals.

pardes.body: A campaign report in five movements. The heading dates it (verse 1); a burst of titles declares who was called on (2 to 4); the speaker sinks under water and rope until he shouts (5 to 7); God comes down in a storm that dismantles the landscape (8 to 16); and one hand pulls one man out of the water (17 to 20). The rest is aftermath: a legal claim that the rescue was deserved (21 to 25), a general rule about how God meets people (26 to 31), then training, battle, pursuit and dominion (32 to 46), closing in praise (47 to 51). Two structural facts do the work. First, the distress of verse 7 is built on the root meaning narrow and the rescue of verse 20 on the root meaning wide, so the whole first half is a movement from a tight place to an open one. Second, verse 39 puts the enemies under my feet, and verse 10 had put thick darkness under His feet; the psalm arranges its own echo and does not comment on it.

This poem exists twice in the Bible, here and as 2 Samuel 22, and the two copies differ from each other in wording and spelling from beginning to end. The most visible consequence is liturgical: Grace after Meals ends with this psalm's last verse on ordinary days, using the participle {{51.0}}, and switches to the noun form of the parallel verse in Samuel on Shabbat and festivals, so a diner meets both versions of the same line in one week. Four cruxes are worth marking. The verb {{2.1}} is the ordinary root for compassion, but in a stem it almost never takes elsewhere in the Bible, which is why translations range from I love You to I am moved toward You. The word {{5.4}} is usually explained as worthlessness or as something like without escape, and it later hardens into a proper name for a demonic figure; the derivation is disputed. In verse 15 the single word {{15.4}} can be read as an adjective, lightnings in abundance, or as a verb, He shot, and both readings are in print. Hardest is {{36.6}} in verse 36: it is derived either from the root for answering or from the root for lowliness, giving either Your response or Your stooping made me great, and no reading has won.

Verses 26 and 27 are the passage everything else in the psalm gets read through. Four times the same construction appears: an adjective describing a person, then a verb built from that adjective in the stem that means to act a quality out, with God as its subject. With the faithful You act faithfully, with the pure You act purely, and then, without warning, with the crooked You act twisted. Read plainly it says God takes the moral shape of whoever approaches Him. The traditional handling of the last clause is to make it a description of consequence rather than of God's nature: a crooked person meets a world that keeps turning out crooked, and the crookedness he meets is his own returned. The same logic organises the two halves of the psalm. In verse 7 the speaker cries out and is heard; in verse 42 his enemies cry out with the same verb and are not answered. Read against verse 21, where the speaker claims the rescue was earned, the psalm is arguing that deliverance is not arbitrary favour but a mirror. Note also that the lamp of {{29.3}} is not a stray image: elsewhere in the historical books God promises David a lamp in Jerusalem, meaning a surviving descendant on the throne, which is where verse 51 ends up.

The theophany hides more than it reveals, and it says so. In verse 12 God makes {{12.1}}, darkness, into a hiding place and pitches it as a shelter, so the closer He comes the less can be seen; the light of verse 13 arrives only as a brightness breaking out of cloud from the inside. Mystical reading takes this as the standing rule for divine approach: concealment is not the absence of presence but its working condition, and the storm is a garment. The cherub of {{11.2}} places the psalm in the same image family as the chariot vision of Ezekiel, the text that later becomes the seed of merkavah mysticism, and here that chariot is in motion for the sake of one drowning man. The pivot at verse 16 belongs to the same reading: the moment the world is stripped to its foundations is also the moment the psalm stops saying He and starts saying You, so the undoing of the created order and the arrival of direct address are described as one event. Verse 51 then extends the whole thing past the speaker, from the anointed king to his seed forever, which is how the poem stops being one man's rescue.
